body:
Folk music in Gujarat's social and cultural life

The folk songs of Gujarat reflect its agricultural life, pastoral communities, religious festivals, marriages and regional traditions. Saurashtra, Kachchh, northern Gujarat, central Gujarat and the tribal regions have their own distinctive repertoires.

Traditional performers, including Charans, Gadhavis and other hereditary or community-based singers, have contributed to the preservation of devotional songs, heroic narratives, historical memories and regional poetry.

Garba and Garbi

Garba is a major Gujarati tradition combining music, dance and religious devotion. It is particularly associated with Navaratri and the worship of the feminine divine power, or Shakti.

The traditional ritual form commonly involves participants singing and dancing around a perforated earthen pot containing a lamp, or around a representation of the goddess. The illuminated pot is traditionally associated with life and divine energy.

The songs accompanying Garba express devotion, celebrate the goddess and reflect collective festive life. Garba therefore belongs simultaneously to Gujarat's folk dance, music and devotional heritage.

UNESCO recognition

Garba of Gujarat was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2023. The inscription recognizes the living practice of Garba, including the knowledge, participation and cultural traditions associated with it.

Its transmission through family and community participation, observation and repeated practice is an important part of its significance as intangible cultural heritage.

Garbi

Garbi is a related Gujarati song and poetic tradition. In Gujarati devotional literature, Dayaram is particularly associated with garbis expressing Krishna devotion.

Garba and Garbi have overlapping histories and usages. Their distinction should not be reduced to an absolute rule about the gender of performers.

Raas and Ras Geet

Raas is a traditional group dance-and-music form associated with Krishna's Raas Lila and Gujarat's festive culture. Ras Geet refers to the songs accompanying such traditions.

Dandiya Raas is a prominent form involving wooden sticks. Raas is performed particularly during Janmashtami and Navaratri.

While Garba is closely identified with goddess worship during Navaratri, Raas has a particularly strong historical and devotional association with Krishna. Both traditions involve collective music and dance.

Life-cycle and narrative folk songs

Gujarati folk songs accompany important stages of human life, including birth, marriage and death. Other forms communicate heroic stories, ethical values and memories of regional history.

FormMeaning or association
Halardu or HalardaLullaby sung to a child
Lagna GeetMarriage songs accompanying wedding customs
FatanaHumorous and teasing wedding songs
MarasiyaMourning songs or laments
DuhaPoetic couplets associated with oral and bardic traditions
PrabhatiyaMorning devotional songs
Ras GeetSongs associated with Raas

Fatana and wedding traditions

Fatana are playful songs traditionally sung during marriage celebrations. They often involve humorous teasing between the families of the bride and groom. Their primary social purpose is to entertain and encourage interaction during wedding festivities.

Duha and bardic traditions

A Duha is a couplet used in regional poetic and oral traditions. In Gujarat, particularly Saurashtra, Duhas are associated with Charani literature and bardic expression.

Their subjects include generosity, honour, loyalty, ethical conduct and historical remembrance. Their concise structure helps preserve memorable expressions through oral recitation.

Dayro

Dayro, also written Dairo, is a traditional Gujarati gathering in which performers present folk songs, devotional compositions, poetry, stories, humour and accounts of historical personalities.

It is especially associated with Saurashtra's oral and folk literary traditions. Dayro provides a setting in which audiences listen to traditional knowledge and share cultural experiences.

Dayro is not the name of a single song form. It is a broader performance and gathering tradition that may include several types of folk and devotional compositions.

Distinguish the terms

Fatana, Halarda and Marasiya identify particular types of songs. Dayro identifies a performance gathering. Garba and Raas combine singing with collective dance.

Tribal folk music in Gujarat

Tribal communities also preserve distinctive forms of folk singing linked with agriculture, seasonal celebrations, marriage and ritual. In southern Gujarat, including the Dangs, the musical traditions of communities such as the Kukna and Warli include songs connected with Holi and collective festivities.

Such traditions demonstrate that Gujarat's folk music heritage extends beyond its better-known urban and regional festival performances.

Prelims focus

  • Garba: Navaratri, Shakti worship and UNESCO inscription in 2023.
  • Raas: Krishna traditions and collective festive dance.
  • Dayaram: devotional garbi compositions.
  • Fatana: humorous marriage songs; Halarda: lullabies.
  • Marasiya: mourning songs; Duha: bardic couplets.
  • Trap: Dayro is a broader performance gathering, not a single musical composition.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, English edition, Chapter 2, Cultural Heritage of India: Traditional Handicraft and Fine Arts, pp. 15–16; UNESCO, Garba of Gujarat, nomination file 01962, Decision 18.COM 8.B.32; Government of Gujarat, NRI Division, Dance and Music and Entertainment; Bharat Sangraha, Folk Songs of Saurashtra and South Gujarat Littoral; Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Folk Fusion: Celebrating Knowledge and Entertainment in Gujarat's Dairo, December 2023; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Gujarat's Folk Songs, Garba, Raas and Dayro

body:
How musical traditions pass between generations

Oral transmission is the passing of knowledge, stories, songs and cultural practices between people primarily through spoken or sung communication, listening, imitation and memory.

Many Indian folk and devotional songs existed as living performances before they were collected into manuscripts or printed books. Children learned songs from elders, disciples learned compositions from spiritual teachers, and community members learned through participation in festivals and ceremonies.

Repetition makes the words and melodies familiar. Regular performance during festivals and rituals helps preserve the association between a song and its cultural purpose.

Variation within oral traditions

Oral transmission does not always preserve every word or melody in exactly the same form. Performers may adapt expressions to local dialects, incorporate their own experiences or modify compositions according to the occasion.

As a result, a song attributed to a saint-poet may survive in several versions. Such variation is an important characteristic of living oral culture and does not necessarily mean that the underlying tradition has been lost.

The bhajans of Mirabai and the verses attributed to Kabir illustrate this process. Successive generations of singers preserved and transmitted their compositions, sometimes introducing variations.

Oral tradition and written preservation

Oral and written transmission are complementary. A devotional poem may first circulate through singing and subsequently become part of a written collection. The written collection preserves one or more versions, while oral performance continues to maintain the tradition within communities.

The compilation of Tamil devotional hymns, the preservation of Kabir's verses in literary collections and the recording of Gujarati folk songs are examples of this relationship.

Hereditary musical communities

Some folk traditions are maintained by communities in which musical knowledge and occupations pass through families.

Manganiyars of Rajasthan

The Manganiyars are a traditional hereditary community of professional Muslim musicians, particularly associated with western Rajasthan. Their repertoire includes songs concerning weddings, regional heroes, religious devotion and the lives of their patron communities.

The performance of Hindu devotional compositions by Muslim musicians illustrates the interaction between religious traditions in India's regional cultural life.

Kalbelia folk songs and dances

The Kalbelia community of Rajasthan preserves songs and dances that express its cultural identity, traditional occupations and mythological knowledge. These traditions have been maintained substantially through oral transmission.

UNESCO inscribed the Kalbelia folk songs and dances of Rajasthan on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010.

Social functions of folk and devotional music

FunctionIllustrative example
Preservation of historical memoryPowada and Gujarati bardic traditions
Celebration of agricultural and seasonal lifeBihu Geet and Kajri
Marking important life eventsSohar, Lagna Geet and Marasiya
Religious worshipBhajan, kirtan and Shabad Kirtan
Spiritual and ethical instructionGangasati's bhajans and Kabir's verses
Community participation and identityGarba and Kalbelia traditions
Communication of sacred narrativesPandavani and Harikatha
Traditional livelihoodManganiyar musicians

These functions often coexist. A single folk performance may entertain an audience, preserve local history, express devotion and provide a livelihood to performers.

Jhaverchand Meghani and the preservation of Gujarati folk literature

Jhaverchand Meghani (1896–1947) was a major Gujarati writer, poet and collector of folk literature. He made an important contribution to preserving the oral cultural traditions of Gujarat, especially Saurashtra.

Meghani collected songs, ballads, stories, lullabies, devotional compositions and other forms of folk expression from living communities and presented them in published collections.

CollectionPrincipal subject
Radhiyali RaatTraditional Gujarati folk songs, including Raas and Garba songs
ChundadiGujarati marriage songs
HalardaLullabies
Rutu GeetoSeasonal songs
Sorathi SantvaniDevotional songs and saint-poet traditions of Saurashtra
Sorathiya DuhaRegional couplets

The significance of these collections lies in their preservation of cultural expressions that might otherwise remain known only to particular communities or disappear when the circumstances of oral transmission change.

A collector or compiler of folk songs is not necessarily their original composer. Meghani preserved and edited numerous compositions that had already circulated among Gujarati communities.

Recognition as intangible cultural heritage

Intangible cultural heritage includes living knowledge, skills, oral traditions, performing arts, rituals and social practices that communities recognize as part of their cultural heritage.

Unlike a monument or archaeological object, an oral musical tradition survives principally through the people who know, perform and transmit it. Written collections and recordings support its preservation, but continued practice remains essential.

The following musical and performance traditions are listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, with their inscription years and country associations verified as of 26 November 2026.

TraditionCountry of inscriptionYear
Baul songsBangladesh2008
Kalbelia folk songs and dances of RajasthanIndia2010
Sankirtana of ManipurIndia2013
Garba of GujaratIndia2023

These inscriptions recognize living cultural practices rather than physical sites. They encourage safeguarding, transmission and recognition of cultural diversity. They do not establish exclusive national ownership of a tradition that may extend across geographical boundaries.

Prelims focus

  • Oral transmission permits variation across generations and regions.
  • Manganiyars are traditional professional musicians associated with western Rajasthan.
  • Radhiyali Raat and Chundadi are folk song collections associated with Jhaverchand Meghani.
  • Kalbelia: 2010; Manipuri Sankirtana: 2013; Garba: 2023.
  • Baul songs were inscribed under Bangladesh in 2008.
  • Trap: UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage lists are distinct from the World Heritage List of sites.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapters 8–9, pp. 115–117, 122–125; Rajasthan Tourism, Village of Manganiyars; Rekhta Gujarati, Jhaverchand Meghani Profile and Biography, section on folk song collections; Nalini Natarajan, ed., Handbook of Twentieth-Century Literatures of India, p. 114; UNESCO, Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, Article 2; UNESCO nomination files 00107, 00340, 00843 and 01962; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
